content: The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) conducts an annual review of the recommended Adult Immunization Schedule to ensure it aligns with the most current recommendations for licensed vaccines. In October 2009, ACIP approved the Adult Immunization Schedule for 2010, which included several updates. A bivalent human papillomavirus vaccine (HPV2) was licensed for use in females in October 2009. ACIP recommends vaccination of females with either HPV2 or the quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccine (HPV4). HPV4 was also licensed for use in males in October 2009, and ACIP issued a permissive recommendation for its use in males. Introductory clarifications were added to the footnotes for vaccines against measles, mumps, rubella, influenza, pneumococcal disease, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and meningococcal disease. For the meningococcal vaccine, the footnote specifies which vaccine formulations are preferred for adults aged ≤55 years and ≥56 years, and which formulations can be used for revaccination. New examples were included to clarify who should and should not be considered for revaccination. The Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine footnote identifies high-risk individuals eligible to receive one dose of the Hib vaccine. The Recommended Adult Immunization Schedule has been approved by ACIP, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the American College of Physicians. Adults with uncertain or incomplete histories of primary vaccination with tetanus and diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccines should begin or complete a primary vaccination series. A primary series for adults consists of three doses of tetanus and diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccines: the first two doses should be administered at least four weeks apart, and the third dose should be given 6–12 months after the second dose. Tdap can substitute for any one of the doses in the three-dose primary series. A booster dose of tetanus and diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine should be administered to adults who have completed a primary series if the last vaccination was received ≥10 years previously. Either Tdap or Td vaccine may be used, as indicated. For pregnant women, if the last Td vaccination was received ≥10 years previously, Td should be administered during the second or third trimester. If the last Td vaccination was received <10 years previously, Tdap should be administered during the immediate postpartum period. A dose of Tdap is recommended for postpartum women, close contacts of infants aged <12 months, and all healthcare personnel with direct patient contact if they have not previously received Tdap. An interval as short as two years from the last Td vaccination is suggested, but shorter intervals can be used. Td may be deferred during pregnancy, with Tdap substituted in the immediate postpartum period, or Tdap can be administered instead of Td to a pregnant woman. Consult the ACIP statement for recommendations on using Td as prophylaxis in wound management. HPV vaccination is recommended at age 11 or 12 years, with catch-up vaccination for individuals aged 13 through 26 years. Ideally, the vaccine should be administered before potential exposure to HPV through sexual activity. However, sexually active females should still be vaccinated according to age-based recommendations. Females who have not been infected with any of the HPV vaccine types (types 6, 11, 16, 18 for HPV4; types 16 and 18 for HPV2) receive the full benefit of vaccination. Vaccination is less beneficial for females already infected with one or more HPV vaccine types. HPV4 or HPV2 can be administered to individuals with a history of genital warts, abnormal Pap tests, or positive HPV DNA tests, as these conditions do not indicate prior infection with all vaccine HPV types. HPV4 may be administered to males aged 9 through 26 years to reduce the likelihood of acquiring genital warts. HPV4 is most effective when administered before exposure to HPV through sexual contact. A complete series for either HPV4 or HPV2 consists of three doses: the second dose should be administered 1–2 months after the first dose, and the third dose should be administered six months after the first dose. Although HPV vaccination is not specifically recommended for individuals with certain medical conditions, it may be administered to these individuals because the HPV vaccine is not a live-virus vaccine. However, the immune response and vaccine efficacy may be lower in individuals with these medical conditions compared to immunocompetent individuals. Healthcare personnel are not at increased risk due to occupational exposure and should be vaccinated according to age-based recommendations. All adults without evidence of immunity to varicella should receive two doses of single-antigen varicella vaccine if not previously vaccinated, or a second dose if they have received only one dose, unless they have a medical contraindication. Pregnant women should be assessed for evidence of varicella immunity. Women without evidence of immunity should receive the first dose of varicella vaccine upon completion or termination of pregnancy and before discharge from the healthcare facility. The second dose should be administered 4–8 weeks after the first dose. A single dose of zoster vaccine is recommended for adults aged ≥60 years, regardless of whether they report a prior episode of herpes zoster. Individuals with chronic medical conditions may be vaccinated unless their condition constitutes a contraindication. Adults born before 1957 are generally considered immune to measles and mumps. Adults born during or after 1957 should receive one or more doses of MMR vaccine unless they have a medical contraindication, documentation of vaccination, laboratory evidence of immunity, or physician-diagnosed measles or mumps. A second dose of MMR vaccine, administered four weeks after the first dose, is recommended for adults in specific high-risk groups, such as those exposed to measles or mumps, healthcare workers, international travelers, and students in postsecondary educational institutions. Hepatitis A vaccination is recommended for individuals with specific risk factors, such as international travelers to countries with high or intermediate endemicity, and for anyone seeking protection from hepatitis A virus infection. The vaccine should be administered in a two-dose schedule, with the second dose given 6–12 months (Havrix) or 6–18 months (Vaqta) after the first dose. If the combined hepatitis A and hepatitis B vaccine (Twinrix) is used, administer three doses at 0, 1, and 6 months, or a four-dose schedule on days 0, 7, and 21–30, followed by a booster dose at month 12. Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for individuals with specific risk factors, such as healthcare personnel, individuals with chronic liver disease, and international travelers to countries with high or intermediate prevalence of chronic HBV infection. A three-dose series should be administered, with the second dose given one month after the first dose and the third dose at least two months after the second dose (and at least four months after the first dose). For patients receiving hemodialysis or with other immunocompromising conditions, higher-dose formulations or alternative schedules may be used. Meningococcal vaccination is recommended for individuals with specific medical conditions, such as asplenia or complement component deficiencies, and for travelers to areas with high meningococcal disease risk, such as the meningitis belt of sub-Saharan Africa. Vaccination is also required for travelers to Mecca during the annual Hajj.
